verdict.winner: Spray foam wins on built-in insulation; TPO wins on lower maintenance and year-round install.
verdict.reasoning: Choose spray polyurethane foam over TPO when the deck needs added thermal performance in minimal height — SPF's R-6.0–6.5 per inch (ICC-ES/SPFA) builds insulation into the membrane, where TPO carries none and depends on separate polyiso boards.
verdict.alternate: Choose TPO over spray polyurethane foam when maintenance burden leads — TPO takes only periodic seam inspection, while SPF takes recoating every 10–20 years to stay UV-protected, per the SPFA.

keyFacts: Spray polyurethane foam adds R-6.0–6.5 per inch of aged insulation, while TPO carries no built-in R-value (per ICC-ES reports and the SPFA).
Spray polyurethane foam installs at $4–$8 per square foot in NJ; TPO runs $8–$12 per square foot over separate polyiso (per commercial cost guides and Josten Roofing, NJ).
SPF carries the lower entry cost because one spray pass lays membrane, insulation, and air barrier together, removing the separate polyiso layer (per commercial cost guides and the SPFA).
TPO costs more per square foot because the system stacks separate polyiso insulation boards beneath the welded membrane, adding material layers and labor (per commercial cost guides).

Spray polyurethane foam is a roof covering of liquid polyurethane that expands into a closed-cell foam, bonds to the substrate, and cures into a seamless, monolithic insulation-and-waterproofing layer under a protective coating; it forms the membrane, insulation, and air barrier in one field-sprayed pass.

TPO is a single-ply thermoplastic-polyolefin membrane, heat-welded at the seams, installed as a reflective, water-shedding surface that carries no built-in R-value and rests over separate insulation boards.
Two inches of SPF foam adds roughly R-12–R-13, measured by the ASTM C1289 LTTR method (per ICC-ES).
NJ's 2021 IECC ceiling insulation target is R-60, which TPO reaches through separate polyiso layers while SPF integrates the air barrier and insulation in the covering (per the 2021 IECC).
White TPO holds a solar reflectance of 0.70–0.85 and a thermal emittance of 0.80–0.90, measured per ASTM C1549 and listed by the CRRC.
A reflective (white TPO) roof cuts peak cooling demand 11–27% in air-conditioned buildings (per the EPA).
A reflective roof stays over 50°F cooler than a conventional roof (per the DOE).

Spray polyurethane foam lasts 30+ years when its coating is maintained; TPO is rated 7–20 years (per the SPFA and the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart), with TPO commonly cited at 15–25 years in practice.
Spray polyurethane foam needs recoating every 10–20 years — acrylic coatings on a 10–15-year cycle, silicone on a 15–20-year cycle — to keep the UV-sensitive foam protected (per the SPFA).
TPO requires only periodic seam inspection for maintenance (per NRCA guidance and the SPFA).
SPF failure modes are blistering from trapped moisture or poor prep, adhesion loss, and coating erosion under ponding (per the SPFA and NRCA).
TPO fails most often at the welded seam, then through chemical attack from rooftop equipment and thermal-shock cracking as plasticizers migrate (per NRCA technical guidance).
SPF is a seamless monolithic spray application; TPO is installed with heat-welded seams (per the SPFA and NRCA).
The NRCA requires positive drainage beneath a spray-foam roof to prevent coating erosion and blistering; TPO drains to outlets (per NRCA guidance).
SPF is a weather-sensitive field-spray application with a narrower NJ installation window, while heat-welded TPO installs year-round including in cold weather (per the SPFA and NRCA).
sources: N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 (NJ Uniform Construction Code, including 5:23-2.7(b) and 5:23-2.7(c))
njContext: Spray polyurethane foam installs at $4–$8 per square foot in NJ; TPO runs $8–$12 per square foot over separate polyiso (per commercial cost guides and Josten Roofing, NJ).
The NJ Uniform Construction Code classifies a spray-foam or TPO re-roof as ordinary maintenance only on a detached 1- or 2-family dwelling (per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7).

Most commercial flat roofs require a NJ permit when roof work exceeds 25% of roof area in 12 months, since the ordinary-maintenance exemption covers only detached 1- and 2-family dwellings (per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7(c)).
Structural work — replacing rafters, decking, or beams — always triggers NJ UCC review (per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7(b) and 5:23-2.7(c)).

SPF's weather-sensitive field spray narrows its NJ installation window relative to year-round heat-welded TPO, a scheduling difference across a north-NJ winter's roughly 35–45 freeze-thaw cycles (regional estimate).

For an Essex County flat-roof home, SPF suits height-restricted decks (delivers R-6.0–6.5 per inch in minimal thickness where polyiso stacks raise the deck past door thresholds), while TPO suits standard residential flat sections at lower upkeep (per ICC-ES, the SPFA, and NRCA guidance).

For a commercial flat roof, SPF fits insulation-driven decks where NRCA-required positive drainage exists, while TPO fits reflectance-driven new low-slope decks where the white membrane's 0.70–0.85 solar reflectance cuts peak cooling demand 11–27% and year-round welding shortens the tenant-disruption window (per ASTM C1549, the EPA, and NRCA guidance).
positioning: Position Newark Quality Roofing as a registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136), insured, offering a free written estimate for Essex County flat-roof projects. NQR assesses the building — deck condition, height/threshold constraints, drainage, insulation needs, and rooftop traffic/equipment — to determine whether SPF or TPO delivers better value, and coordinates the NJ UCC permit path (ordinary-maintenance exemption vs. the 25%-of-roof-area commercial trigger under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7). Frame warranty honestly as two parts: the manufacturer's material warranty on the membrane/coating plus NQR's written workmanship warranty on the install — never as manufacturer certification tiers. NJ has no roofing contractor license; describe NQR as registered, not 'licensed.'
defabToKill: buyers-guide — 'SPF provides the highest R-value per inch of any commercial insulation (R-6.5 per inch)': 'highest of any commercial insulation' superlative is not in the gold (gold states R-6.0–6.5 per inch per ICC-ES/SPFA, no superlative). Dies; restate the gold range with source, drop the superlative.

buyers-guide — 'requires recoating every 10-15 years. Each recoating costs $2-$4 per square foot': the $2–$4/sq ft recoat cost is invented — not in the gold (gold gives no recoat dollar figure; recoat cycle is 10–20 years per SPFA, not 10–15). Dies as invented figure + wrong cycle.

buyers-guide — 'SPF roofs are vulnerable to bird damage, hail, and foot traffic ... foam surface is softer than TPO': bird/hail/foot-traffic vulnerability claims are not substantiated in the gold (gold failure modes are blistering, adhesion loss, coating erosion). Dies unless reframed to gold-listed failure modes.
buyers-guide — 'SPF self-flashes ... complex geometry with many penetrations': the self-flashing penetration claim is not in the gold. Dies; gold supports 'seamless monolithic' only.

buyers-guide — 'SPF runs $5-$9 per square foot installed. TPO with insulation runs $6-$11 per square foot': invented cost ranges — contradict the gold's verified $4–$8 (SPF) and $8–$12 (TPO) per Josten Roofing/commercial cost guides. Dies; replace with gold figures + source.

buyers-guide — 'when you factor in the energy savings from SPF superior insulation, the lifetime cost may favor SPF': speculative lifetime-cost/energy-savings math not in the gold, plus 'superior' superlative + 'may' modality. Dies (de-fab + modality).
buyers-guide — 'walk-ability ... walk pads around equipment to prevent foam compression damage': foam-compression / walk-pad claims are not in the gold. Dies as unsubstantiated.

Dies; restate the gold's directional fact, no fabricated month range.

expert-picks — 'Wind is SPF's other enemy ... overspray issues that affect neighboring properties ... We schedule SPF applications only on calm days': fabricated NQR scheduling anecdote + wind/overspray claim not in the gold. Dies.

Buildings that skipped scheduled recoating show foam degradation ... sometimes severe enough to require partial re-spraying': fabricated NQR project-history / observation. Dies; reframe to SPFA recoat cycle + UV-sensitivity facts.

TPO is our default commercial recommendation for Essex County': first-person 'we recommend / our default' framing presented as field judgment. Dies; reframe as what the standards/specs favor, then NQR's honest registered-NJ-HIC assessment.

BOTH — no 'licensed contractor' / 'NJ-licensed' phrasing appears in either dirty article, but ctaText/positioning must use 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor' (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136), never 'licensed' — NJ has no roofing license.

CURRENCY — neither article cites the 30% federal solar ITC / §25D / §25C, ENERGY STAR roof program, R-49 code, or NJ historic tax credit; none present, so none to kill here. Cooling-demand reflectance is correctly the EPA 11–27% figure (gold), not an invented 'AC savings %.'

buyersGuide.h1: Which Is Better: Spray Foam vs TPO?
buyersGuide.directAnswerThesis: Neither wins outright: spray foam wins when the deck needs built-in R-6.0–6.5-per-inch insulation in minimal height; TPO wins on lower maintenance and year-round install. Insulation need versus upkeep is the deciding factor.
